units.title: Unit 49 — Difficulty
learningObjectives: Recognise degree and severity in collocations that describe disasters, risk and prolonged difficulty.
Choose precise verb–noun partnerships for confronting, managing and overcoming problems.
Replace common non-idiomatic verb combinations with natural English patterns for problems and solutions.
Apply register-sensitive collocations in original professional and everyday situations.

items.example: Balancing two jobs became a constant struggle during her final semester.
items.note: A constant struggle emphasises repeated effort over a prolonged period; it is stronger than an occasional difficulty.

items.example: The contradictory announcements left the audience in a state of confusion.
items.note: Use in a state of confusion to describe general uncertainty when people do not know what to do.

items.example: The cancellation of the grant was a severe blow to the research team.
items.note: A severe blow is an event that seriously damages hopes, confidence or prospects, not necessarily a physical impact.

items.example: The mountain rescue was delayed by adverse weather conditions.
items.note: Formal wording for unfavourable weather, especially in travel, safety and official reports.

items.example: Several villages reported widespread flooding after the river burst its banks.
items.note: Widespread means affecting many places or people rather than a single isolated location.

items.example: The authorities introduced extra patrols after reports of widespread looting.
items.note: Looting means stealing property during disorder or a disaster; widespread highlights its extent.

items.example: The hikers were in grave danger once the storm reached the ridge.
items.note: Grave intensifies the seriousness of danger; it is more formal and stronger than ordinary danger.

items.example: There is a high risk of delays when every task depends on one supplier.
items.note: High is a natural modifier of risk, especially when discussing probability or exposure.

items.example: The outdoor concert turned into a complete disaster when the power failed.
items.note: Complete is an emphatic, often conversational modifier of disaster.

items.example: Ignoring the structural warning signs could have catastrophic results.
items.note: Catastrophic describes extremely serious consequences, not merely disappointing outcomes.

items.example: Restoring the historic theatre required months of hard work.
items.note: Hard work means demanding effort; it is normally uncountable in this sense.

items.example: Small firms often face a problem when a major client pays late.
items.note: Face a problem means confront an existing difficulty; face does not imply that a solution has been found.

items.example: The committee agreed to address the problem before approving the budget.
items.note: Address a problem means give it attention and take steps towards resolving it; common in professional settings.

items.example: A cross-functional team was formed to tackle the problem of slow deliveries.
items.note: Tackle implies active and determined efforts, often involving a difficult or complex issue.

items.example: The invasive species may pose a threat to native birds.
items.note: Pose a threat is a conventional way to say that something creates a potential danger.

items.example: Any investment with unusually high returns will also carry a risk.
items.note: Carry a risk means involve or entail exposure to possible harm or loss.

items.example: Regular backups help minimise the risk of permanent data loss.
items.note: Minimise the risk means reduce likelihood or exposure as far as reasonably possible; it does not promise zero risk.

items.example: Our new project manager seems to relish a challenge rather than avoid it.
items.note: Relish means take genuine pleasure in something, so relish a challenge signals a positive attitude.

items.example: Unclear responsibilities can hinder progress even in a skilled team.
items.note: Hinder progress means slow down or obstruct advancement, rather than necessarily stop it entirely.

items.example: The editor spotted an error in the figures before the report was printed.
items.note: Spot an error suggests noticing or detecting it, often through careful observation.

items.example: New users may encounter difficulties during the initial configuration.
items.note: Encounter difficulties describes coming across obstacles, sometimes unexpectedly; register is fairly formal.

items.example: The legal team had to deal with the complexities of international licensing.
items.note: Deal with the complexities of something stresses handling its many connected details.

items.example: The start-up overcame hurdles to bring its first device to market.
items.note: A hurdle is an obstacle; overcome hurdles emphasises successfully moving beyond barriers.

items.example: Small coastal businesses had to fight for survival after the harbour closed.
items.note: Fight for survival expresses an intense effort to continue existing in very difficult conditions.

items.example: The local volunteers were trained to respond to an emergency quickly.
items.note: Respond to an emergency is standard language for taking action when an urgent situation occurs.

items.example: When disaster strikes, a reliable communication plan can save lives.
items.note: Disaster strikes is a common fixed pattern for the sudden occurrence of a serious event.

items.example: It is easy to make a mistake when several files have similar names.
items.note: The normal verb is make, not do, in the collocation make a mistake.

items.example: We have problems with connectivity whenever the building loses power.
items.note: Use have problems, rather than get problems, to describe continuing difficulties.

items.example: Several passengers experienced difficulties when changing their bookings.
items.note: Experience difficulties is a natural, relatively formal alternative to have difficulties.

items.example: The engineers worked together to find a solution to the overheating issue.
items.note: We usually find or develop a solution; give a solution is not the usual verb choice here.

items.example: If problems arise during installation, contact the support team.
items.note: Problems arise or occur naturally; happen is much less idiomatic with problems.

items.example: Difficulties may arise if the timetable changes at short notice.
items.note: Difficulties arise is a natural pattern; difficulties appear is generally less idiomatic.

items.example: Serious problems can occur when the system is not maintained.
items.note: Problems occur is an alternative to problems arise and sounds neutral or formal.

items.example: The proposal encountered resistance from several department heads.
items.note: Encounter resistance describes opposition met while trying to introduce an idea or change.

items.example: The working group will tackle the issue of unequal access to training.
items.note: Tackle an issue means address a matter through purposeful action, not just discuss it.

items.example: The newly appointed director was asked to tackle a crisis in funding.
items.note: Tackle a crisis suggests urgent, active intervention in an especially serious problem.

items.example: The unexpected observation poses a question about the original theory.
items.note: Pose a question means raise it for consideration; it is more formal than ask a question.

items.example: The lack of wheelchair access poses a problem for many visitors.
items.note: Pose a problem means create a difficulty or obstacle in a particular situation.

units.title: Unit 50 — Quantity and size
learningObjectives: Distinguish countable and uncountable noun patterns with informal and formal quantifiers.
Use idiomatic collocations for exceptionally large sizes, amounts, numbers and varieties.
Choose adjective partners such as small, large, high and great in their natural combinations.
Interpret figurative quantity expressions and recognise their register and pragmatic effect.

items.example: A good few applicants already have experience with the software.
items.note: Informal quantifier used before a plural countable noun; it means considerably more than just a few.

items.example: A fair few neighbours attended the planning meeting.
items.note: Fair few is informal and applies to plural countable nouns, not mass nouns.

items.example: A good number of residents volunteered for the clean-up.
items.note: An informal expression for quite a large number of separate people or things.

items.example: A fair number of readers requested a longer explanation.
items.note: A fair number of takes plural countable nouns and is less formal than a significant number of.

items.example: A substantial number of employees supported the revised schedule.
items.note: Substantial number of is formal and describes a considerable count of individual items or people.

items.example: A significant number of patients reported an improvement in sleep quality.
items.note: Use number with plural countable nouns; significant often signals an important or sizable count.

items.example: The expedition stored a substantial quantity of drinking water.
items.note: Quantity of fits mass nouns such as water or fuel; the phrase has a formal tone.

items.example: The factory recovered a significant quantity of usable material.
items.note: A formal way to refer to a large quantity of something treated as uncountable.

items.example: The repairs will require a substantial amount of time.
items.note: Amount of is generally used with uncountable nouns such as time, money or effort.

items.example: The charity received a significant amount of funding from local businesses.
items.note: Significant amount of is formal; use it with mass nouns rather than plural countable items.

items.example: The sheer quantity of applications surprised the admissions team.
items.note: Sheer emphasises striking or overwhelming size, not simply a statistically large value.

items.example: There is a finite number of places available in the workshop.
items.note: Finite means limited; number is followed by a plural countable noun.

items.example: The meeting room is a good size for a team of ten.
items.note: A good size generally means pleasantly or sufficiently large, not an exact measurement.

items.example: She brought unbounded enthusiasm to the community theatre project.
items.note: Unbounded means apparently without limits and creates an emphatic positive description.

items.example: Teaching beginners often requires infinite patience.
items.note: Infinite is an expressive exaggeration of limitless patience, not a literal measurement.

items.example: The volunteers seemed to have an endless supply of creative ideas.
items.note: An endless supply suggests so much is available that it appears never to run out.

items.example: Some private consultants charge astronomical fees for a brief consultation.
items.note: Astronomical describes a surprisingly or excessively high amount, especially a price or fee.

items.example: The farm reported a bumper crop of strawberries after a mild spring.
items.note: Bumper crop is a notably large or successful agricultural harvest.

items.example: The transport disruption reached epic proportions during the holiday weekend.
items.note: Epic proportions emphasises extreme scale, often of a problem or unusual event.

items.example: The investigation confirmed that the patient had suffered a massive overdose.
items.note: Massive strongly intensifies overdose; avoid using the phrase for ordinary medication doses.

items.example: An overwhelming majority of members voted for the new constitution.
items.note: Overwhelming majority means a very large majority, clearly greater than a narrow margin.

items.example: The team spent an inordinate amount of time searching for lost documents.
items.note: Inordinate means larger than reasonable or appropriate; it usually implies criticism.

items.example: The sheer size of the warehouse made navigation difficult.
items.note: Sheer size highlights astonishment at how big something is.

items.example: The museum offers a wide range of workshops for local schools.
items.note: Wide range refers to diversity of options or types, not the quantity of one substance.

items.example: The market sells a wide variety of locally grown vegetables.
items.note: Wide variety emphasises many different kinds within a category.

items.example: The online platform gives learners a wide choice of practice activities.
items.note: Wide choice stresses the availability of many options to select from.

items.example: The new supplier is still an unknown quantity to our purchasing team.
items.note: Idiomatic phrase for a person or factor whose ability or characteristics have not been established.

items.example: A small minority of residents opposed the renovation.
items.note: Small, rather than little, is the standard adjective with minority.

items.example: Only a small amount of paint remained in the tin.
items.note: Small amount is natural with an uncountable substance; avoid little amount.

items.example: A small number of tickets were returned before the event.
items.note: With number, use small for a low count; little number is not idiomatic.

items.example: A small quantity of powder was set aside for testing.
items.note: Small quantity combines naturally with an uncountable material.

items.example: A small percentage of users selected the premium option.
items.note: Small percentage expresses a low share; little percentage is not natural.

items.example: A large majority of the board approved the merger.
items.note: Large majority is possible; great majority is less idiomatic in this teaching context.

items.example: A large number of passengers were affected by the cancellation.
items.note: Large number is a conventional choice for countable things; avoid big number here in formal prose.

items.example: The company imported a large quantity of recycled steel.
items.note: Large is the natural adjective with quantity in standard quantity descriptions.

items.example: A large amount of energy is lost through poor insulation.
items.note: Large amount works with mass nouns; big amount is generally less suitable.

items.example: A large percentage of customers renew their subscriptions.
items.note: Both large percentage and high percentage are natural; great percentage is not.

items.example: A high percentage of participants completed the survey.
items.note: High percentage is a standard numerical expression; high does not generally pair with amount or quantity.

items.example: The committee attached great importance to transparent selection criteria.
items.note: Great importance is idiomatic; high importance is usually less natural in ordinary prose.

items.example: The discovery has great significance for coastal ecology.
items.note: Great significance conveys considerable importance and is more natural than big significance.

items.example: The elder was respected for her seemingly infinite wisdom.
items.note: Infinite wisdom can be sincere or ironic depending on tone and context.

items.example: The new materials opened up endless possibilities for designers.
items.note: Endless possibilities evokes a very wide range of potential outcomes or choices.

items.example: After years abroad, she felt an overwhelming desire to return home.
items.note: Overwhelming desire is a feeling so strong that it is difficult to ignore.

items.example: The organisation needed to distribute food on a massive scale.
items.note: On a massive scale means carried out across a very large area, population or volume.

items.example: Their epic journey across the desert became a documentary.
items.note: Epic journey conveys unusual length, effort or dramatic importance.

items.example: The workers faced an epic struggle to protect the endangered forest.
items.note: Epic struggle conveys prolonged, difficult and often heroic effort.

items.example: The report said the actor had suffered a massive heart attack.
items.note: Massive heart attack is an established phrase for a very severe cardiac event; used cautiously in health contexts.

items.example: Endless arguments over minor details delayed the team’s decision.
items.note: Endless arguments emphasises repeated or apparently never-ending disputes.
